title: The Cutter Race and the Cairn of Skis: Scott, the Discovery, and the Pole Reached Second
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Outlands, Stoke Damerel: the brewer's son
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott', gives 6 June 1868 at Outlands, Stoke Damerel, near Devonport, and the dossier agrees independently. The coordinate is the Milehouse district of Plymouth where the estate stood; the house itself was demolished and the pin is to the district, not to a surviving building.
stops.campa: At Outlands, a small estate at Stoke Damerel above the Devonport dockyards, Hannah Cuming Scott bears a third child and names him Robert Falcon. His father John Edward Scott owns a brewery and lives as a country gentleman on its income. Four of the six children are girls, and both boys are promised to the services from infancy. The windows look toward the Hamoaze and the masts of the western fleet. The boy is small, sickly, slow at his lessons and given to daydreaming, and the family remembers him afterwards as the one who had to be pushed.
suggested_refs: The Milehouse district of Plymouth, site of the demolished Outlands estate

stops.name: Stubbington, Hampshire: the naval crammer
stops.date_confidence: traditional as to the years. That Scott was sent to Stubbington House School to prepare for the naval entrance examination is attested (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'); the span of roughly 1877 to 1881 comes from Plymouth local-history material relayed by the dossier and is not independently corroborated, so the month and day default to 1 January. The coordinate has been corrected: an earlier fix placed the school about 2 km southwest in the Hill Head direction.
stops.campa: Sent inland to Hampshire at about nine, he boards at Stubbington House, the crammer that Navy families use to force their sons through the entrance examination. The regime is arithmetic, navigation and Latin, drilled at speed against a fixed date. The school exists to deliver thirteen-year-olds to a training ship in fit condition to be examined, and it stands a few miles from the Solent, close enough for the boys to hear the fleet exercising. Nothing in the reachable record says whether he was happy there. It says he passed.
suggested_refs: Stubbington House School, Hampshire, the 'Naval Academy' that prepared cadets for HMS Britannia
sources: robert_falcon_scott.dossier.md (Plymouth local-history material, uncorroborated for exact years)

stops.name: The River Dart: cadet aboard HMS Britannia
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1881 for entry and to July 1883 for passing out seventh of twenty-six (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'). The precise day of entry, 15 July, comes from the geography lens and is not separately corroborated in this pass.
stops.campa: He joins the cadet training ship Britannia, an old wooden three-decker moored in the Dart, at thirteen. Two years of seamanship, gunnery and mathematics follow, lived aboard in hammocks under a deck built for a ship of the line. He passes out in July 1883, seventh in a class of twenty-six, and goes into the fleet as a midshipman: competent, unremarkable, and now the property of the Royal Navy for the rest of his working life. He is fifteen years old.
suggested_refs: HMS Britannia, cadet training ship moored on the River Dart before the Royal Naval College was built ashore

stops.name: Basseterre, St Kitts: the morning race across the bay
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 March 1887 at St Kitts (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'; dossier citing Markham's own recollections). One correction stands: the ship was HMS Rover, attached to the Training Squadron, not the West Indies squadron as an earlier draft of the chronology had it. Markham was Secretary of the Royal Geographical Society at this date and became its President only in 1893.
stops.campa: His cutter wins the morning race across the bay, and a passenger in the squadron notices. Clements Markham, Secretary of the Royal Geographical Society, collects promising young officers the way other men collect stamps, and keeps a private list of those he thinks might one day command a polar expedition. He talks to the eighteen-year-old midshipman at dinner, and afterwards writes the name down in the list. Twelve years pass before anything comes of it.
suggested_refs: Clements Markham's own recollections of the 1887 cutter race, the origin story of the Discovery command

stops.name: Portsmouth, HMS Vernon: torpedo school and the family's ruin
stops.date_confidence: the two lenses contradicted each other and the contradiction is resolved here in favour of the geography lens: 1891 is when Scott applied for and began the two-year torpedo course, graduating with first-class certificates in 1893 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'). A chronology entry dating completion to 1891 was wrong. The family's financial collapse is dated c. 1894 and the Shepton Mallet removal to c. 1894-1897 from the dossier, not independently re-verified against a primary record.
stops.campa: He applies for the two-year torpedo course at Vernon, the Navy's school for its newest and most technical branch, and comes out with first-class certificates in theory and practice. It marks him as a modern officer rather than a seaman of the old kind. In the same years the family money goes. His father sells the brewery, invests the proceeds badly, and by 1894 the Scotts are reduced, John Edward taking a salaried post as a brewery manager at Shepton Mallet. The lieutenant's pay becomes a household's income. His father dies in 1897, his brother Archie of typhoid in 1898, and Scott is left with his mother and sisters to keep.
suggested_refs: The Shepton Mallet brewery where John Edward Scott took paid work after losing the family capital
sources: robert_falcon_scott.dossier.md, on the Scott family finances

segments.name: The Chance Encounter and the Discovery

stops.name: London, Markham's door: the volunteering
stops.date_confidence: attested but split. Two distinct events had been collapsed into one date in the chronology: the chance street encounter with Clements Markham was early June 1899, usually given as the fifth, and Scott appeared at the Markham residence and volunteered to lead the expedition on 11 June 1899 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'). This stop is dated to the volunteering. The coordinate is Markham's Eccleston Square address and is approximate to the square rather than to a door.
stops.campa: Home on leave in early June, he meets Clements Markham by chance in a London street, twelve years after the cutter race, and hears that a National Antarctic Expedition is being fitted out and has not settled on a commander. He appears at Markham's door on the eleventh and volunteers. He has no polar experience, no scientific training, no private money, and a career that has stalled at lieutenant. What he has is a torpedo certificate and the fact that an old man once watched him win a boat race. Markham backs him within the week.
suggested_refs: Clements Markham's residence at 21 Eccleston Square, London, where Scott volunteered

stops.name: Dundee: the ship built to be squeezed
stops.date_confidence: attested that RRS Discovery was built at the Dundee Shipbuilders Company yard and launched in March 1901 (Discovery Point / RRS Discovery history; Wikipedia). The stop is dated to the construction period with month and day defaulting to 1 January; the coordinate is the present Discovery Point berth, which is the yard's site.
stops.campa: The Dundee Shipbuilders Company lays down a wooden barque-rigged steamer designed to be squeezed rather than crushed: an overhanging bow to ride up onto pressure ice, no external projections for floes to catch, an engine and rudder that can be lifted clear. She is the last three-masted wooden ship built in Britain. Launched in March 1901 and named Discovery, she costs more than the expedition can comfortably afford. The Royal Society and the Royal Geographical Society quarrel over who is to command her, the scientists or the sailors, and Markham wins that argument for Scott.
suggested_refs: RRS Discovery, preserved afloat at Discovery Point, Dundee, on the site of the yard that built her

stops.name: East India Docks, London: Discovery sails south
stops.date_confidence: attested. Discovery left the East India Docks on 31 July 1901 and sailed from Cowes on 6 August after the King's inspection; the chronology lens dates the departure to Cowes and the two are the same voyage a week apart. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from ernest_shackleton.journey.json, which fixes this pin for the atlas.
stops.campa: Discovery clears the East India Docks on the last day of July with Scott, newly promoted commander, in charge, and a third officer out of the merchant service named Ernest Shackleton on her books. On the sixth of August she lies off Cowes and the King comes aboard to inspect her. The command is divided in a way that will never quite be resolved: the Royal Society wants a scientific cruise and Markham wants a naval expedition of discovery. Scott is a torpedo officer who has spent eighteen months reading up on ice.
suggested_refs: The joint Royal Society and Royal Geographical Society instructions to the National Antarctic Expedition, 1901
sources: ernest_shackleton.journey.json, stop 'East India Docks, London: Discovery sails south'

stops.name: Winter Quarters Bay, Ross Island: the ship frozen in
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 February 1902 (Wikipedia, 'Discovery Expedition'). One claim is corrected here: the expedition did not use the shore hut as its headquarters. Scott decided the men should continue to live and work aboard ship and let Discovery freeze into the sea ice, the hut serving as storeroom, shelter and theatre. The coordinate is the atlas's Hut Point pin, about 800 m north of the surveyed 77 degrees 50.9 minutes south.
stops.campa: Discovery works south into McMurdo Sound and puts her bow into a small bay under the volcanic slopes of Ross Island, where she is allowed to freeze in. Scott decides the men will live and work aboard rather than in the prefabricated hut they have carried eleven thousand miles; the hut becomes a storeroom, a shelter and eventually a theatre. The ship is the base. She will not float again for two years. Below decks the men keep their own hammocks and the wardroom stove, and the hut on the shore stands empty except for the stores in it.
suggested_refs: Discovery Hut at Hut Point, built 1902 and still standing, used as store and shelter rather than quarters

stops.name: Hut Point: George Vince goes over the cliff
stops.date_confidence: attested to 11 March 1902 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'). The coordinate is approximate to the ice cliff near Hut Point now called Vince's Cliff; the exact point of the fall is not surveyed.
stops.campa: A sledging party caught in a blizzard on the slopes above the ship loses its footing on ice. George Vince, wearing fur boots with no grip, goes over the edge of a cliff into the sea and is never recovered. It is the expedition's first death, in its first month ashore, within sight of the ship. Scott has men who cannot ski, cannot drive dogs, and do not yet know that weather here arrives in minutes. A wooden cross goes up on the point above the bay that same month, and it is still there.
suggested_refs: The cross to George Vince at Hut Point, the oldest surviving memorial in Antarctica

stops.name: Ross Ice Shelf, 82 degrees 17 minutes south: the record
stops.date_confidence: the Farthest South of the Discovery southern journey is attested to 30 December 1902 (Wikipedia, 'Discovery Expedition'); some chronologies give 14 January 1903, a date that belongs to the return march, and the contradiction is left standing. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from ernest_shackleton.journey.json; longitude there is approximate, the party having turned near Cape Wilson.
stops.campa: Two months out from the ship, Scott, Edward Wilson and Ernest Shackleton stand at 82 degrees 17 minutes south, further than anyone has been, with the Victoria Land mountains on their right hand and the Pole four hundred and sixty miles beyond. The dog driving has failed and the dogs are dying and being fed to one another. They turn north on the thirtieth of December with food for a march that will take longer than the outward one did. All three men have scurvy, and Shackleton is coughing blood.
suggested_refs: Edward Wilson's sketches and Shackleton's photographs of the turning point, later used to recompute the position
sources: ernest_shackleton.journey.json, stop 'Ross Ice Shelf, 82 degrees 17 minutes south: the record'

stops.name: Hut Point: the southern party comes in
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 February 1903 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'). The disagreement between Scott's and Wilson's accounts over who was carried and when is real and is not adjudicated here.
stops.campa: They regain Discovery on the third of February, ninety-three days out, having walked some nine hundred and sixty miles. Shackleton has broken down repeatedly on the Barrier and at times has been carried rather than hauling. Scott has learned that dogs, badly fed and badly driven, kill themselves faster than men do, and he draws from it a general lesson that will cost him: that man-hauling is the honest method and the reliable one. Wilson's diary and Scott's do not agree in every particular about the state of the three of them at the end.
suggested_refs: Edward Wilson's Discovery-expedition diaries, an independent record of the southern journey

stops.name: McMurdo Sound: Shackleton sent home on the Morning
stops.date_confidence: attested that Scott invalided Shackleton home on the relief ship Morning early in 1903; the exact date of Morning's departure is given variously in reachable sources and ernest_shackleton.journey.json sets it to 2 March 1903. The dossier notes that the later 'jealousy' narrative for Scott's motive is uncorroborated, and it is not adopted here.
stops.campa: The relief ship Morning comes in through the pack and Scott sends Shackleton home on her, invalided. Shackleton wants to stay and does not forgive the decision; Scott's account is that the man's health made it necessary, and nobody outside that tent can settle it. Shackleton will come back south on money of his own within five years. Discovery herself stays locked in for a second winter, and it takes explosives, saws and a rising tide the following February to get her out.
suggested_refs: The relief ships Morning and Terra Nova, sent south in 1903-04 to free Discovery from the ice
sources: ernest_shackleton.journey.json, stop 'McMurdo Sound: invalided home on the Morning'

stops.name: Portsmouth: Discovery comes home
stops.date_confidence: attested to 10 September 1904 for the return and the promotion (Wikipedia, 'Discovery Expedition'; dossier adds the London Gazette notice and the CVO). The two-volume narrative is dated 1905 from the dossier, consistent with the well-documented publication history.
stops.campa: Discovery comes home to Portsmouth after three years and Scott steps ashore a public figure. The Admiralty makes him a captain, the King makes him a Commander of the Victorian Order, and the Royal Geographical Society, which had not been sure of him, presents the Furthest South as a British record rather than as a failure to reach a Pole nobody had formally asked him to reach. He finds out what he did not know before: a man who has come back from the ice can raise money. He writes the expedition up in two volumes as The Voyage of the Discovery, published in 1905.
suggested_refs: Robert Falcon Scott, The Voyage of the 'Discovery', 2 vols. (London, 1905)
sources: London Gazette promotion notice, cited in robert_falcon_scott.dossier.md, lines 272-286

segments.name: The Interval: Fleet, Marriage, and the Disputed Ground

stops.name: Portsmouth: the Albemarle collision
stops.date_confidence: dated to 11 February 1907 by the dossier, citing naval archival reassessment; not independently re-verified beyond the dossier in this pass. The collision occurred during fleet manoeuvres at sea and the coordinate is Portsmouth, Albemarle's home port, not the position of the collision.
stops.campa: Back in the ordinary Navy, commanding the battleship Albemarle on fleet manoeuvres, he is involved in a collision with HMS Commonwealth. An inquiry clears him of blame. The episode is small, and it would have been forgotten entirely except that Scott's later detractors go looking for evidence of a careless commander and find it convenient, while his defenders point at the finding. A captain's career in this service can end in an afternoon of bad station-keeping. His does not. He goes back to the fleet, and to the correspondence about a second expedition.
suggested_refs: Admiralty inquiry papers on the Albemarle and Commonwealth collision, February 1907

stops.name: London: meeting Kathleen Bruce
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1907 for the meeting (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'); the month and day are unknown and default to 1 January, and the coordinate is a London placeholder rather than a located venue. The dossier's further claim that Kathleen Bruce trained in Auguste Rodin's orbit could not be confirmed against the atlas's own Rodin file, which names Camille Claudel and other students but not her, and it is therefore not carried as fact.
stops.campa: He meets Kathleen Bruce, a sculptor trained at the Slade and in Paris, at a luncheon party. She is unconventional, poor by choice, entirely outside the naval world, and she has decided in advance that she will bear a son to a remarkable man. The courtship runs mostly by letter and is not smooth; she is being courted by others and says so plainly. He is thirty-nine, a captain without a ship worth having, and the Antarctic is already back in his correspondence. They marry within the year and a half.
suggested_refs: Kathleen Bruce's own memoir Self-Portrait of an Artist (1949), for the courtship correspondence

stops.name: London: the claim on McMurdo Sound
stops.date_confidence: attested as a documented dispute conducted in writing during 1907 and broken in the field in early 1908 (robert_falcon_scott.dossier.md, lines 316-331 and 1023-1029; ernest_shackleton.journey.json, Nimrod stops). The month is set to May 1907 as an ordering device for the correspondence, which ran through that year; no single dated letter anchors this stop. Cape Royds itself is Shackleton's stop and is not staged here.
stops.campa: Shackleton is raising an expedition of his own, and Scott, hearing of it, claims McMurdo Sound as his ground. Shackleton gives him a written undertaking to land east of the 170th meridian and to leave the Sound alone. Ice bars the eastern approaches in 1908 and he breaks the promise, putting his hut at Cape Royds under Erebus, and is reproached for it for the rest of his life. Scott, in England, reads it as a theft of territory. No law of any kind assigns a stretch of Antarctic coast to a British naval captain who wintered there once. Both men proceed as though one did.
suggested_refs: Shackleton's written undertaking to Scott, 1907, on the eastern limit of the Nimrod expedition's landing
sources: ernest_shackleton.journey.json, stop 'Cape Royds, Ross Island: the hut under the volcano'

stops.name: Hampton Court Palace: the Chapel Royal
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2 September 1908 at the Chapel Royal, Hampton Court Palace (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott').
stops.campa: They are married in the Chapel Royal at Hampton Court Palace, in a ceremony arranged around the Navy's convenience and the bride's refusal of most of the conventions. Scott, who has spent his adult life in wardrooms and his childhood among sisters, acquires at forty a household that argues with him. Her letters to him over the next four years are the frankest documents anyone in this story leaves behind, and they push him back toward the ice harder than Markham ever did. Kathleen keeps her studio, her friends and her own working name.
suggested_refs: The Chapel Royal, Hampton Court Palace

stops.name: 174 Buckingham Palace Road: Peter Markham Scott is born
stops.date_confidence: attested to 14 September 1909 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'). The coordinate is corrected from a generic London-centre placeholder to 174 Buckingham Palace Road, the birthplace given precisely in Wikipedia, 'Peter Scott'. The Admiralty appointment as Naval Assistant to the Second Sea Lord is attested to 24 March 1909, earlier the same year, and is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: A son is born at the house in Buckingham Palace Road and is christened Peter Markham Scott, the middle name for the man who found his father at a boat race in St Kitts. Scott had taken a desk at the Admiralty in the spring as Naval Assistant to the Second Sea Lord, and he leaves it before the year is out to organise a second expedition. The boy is two and a half when his father sails, and will not remember him. J. M. Barrie, who stands godfather at the christening, will keep the letter Scott writes him from the tent.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Peter Scott', for the birthplace at 174 Buckingham Palace Road
sources: james_matthew_barrie.journey.json, stop 'The Ross Ice Shelf, the last letter from the tent'

stops.name: Roath Basin, Cardiff: the whaler sails
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 June 1910 for the departure from Cardiff (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'). Scott himself had left London on 1 June 1910 on fundraising business and rejoined the ship later; the dossier notes the earlier London departure and some chronologies give that date instead, which is a conflation of two events.
stops.campa: Terra Nova, a Dundee-built whaler forty years old, warps out of the Roath Basin at Cardiff with the city's coal in her bunkers, given free, and a crowd along the dockside. Scott is not aboard. He has been in London since the first of June chasing the last of the money and will overhaul the ship by faster steamer. The expedition is funded by public subscription, a government grant and personal begging, and it is short of what it needs. Cardiff gets the departure, and by Scott's arrangement it is to get the homecoming too.
suggested_refs: The Roath Basin, Cardiff Docks, and the free coal subscribed by Cardiff owners for the Terra Nova

stops.name: Port Melbourne: the telegram from Christiania
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline to October 1910 (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'; dossier). The exact day the telegram was handed to Scott is not fixed in the reachable sources and the day defaults to the first. Scott had rejoined the ship at Cape Town after travelling south by faster steamer, a rendezvous the dossier and Wikipedia corroborate but which is not given a separate stop here.
stops.campa: Rejoining his ship after a passage by mail steamer, Scott finds a telegram waiting at Melbourne. It is three lines out of Christiania: Amundsen is going south, in the Fram. Amundsen had told the world he was bound for the Arctic and the North Pole, had raised his money on that programme, and changed his object at sea. Scott says publicly that his own plans are unaltered and that the expedition is a scientific one. Aboard the ship the wire is read out and understood otherwise.
suggested_refs: Amundsen's telegram to Scott, Melbourne, October 1910

stops.name: Port Chalmers: the last land
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 November 1910 for the final departure from New Zealand (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'). The details of the gale and the hand-bailing are from the same source and the dossier; the number of animals lost is given consistently as two ponies and a dog.
stops.campa: Terra Nova leaves New Zealand loaded past any reasonable mark: thirty-four dogs, nineteen ponies, three motor sledges, coal in sacks on deck, petrol in cans. Two days out a gale nearly finishes her. The pumps choke on coal dust, the men bail with buckets in a chain through the night, two ponies and a dog are lost, and the ship lives because an officer cuts through a bulkhead to reach the flooded well by hand. Then twenty days jammed in the pack, burning coal she cannot spare.
suggested_refs: Port Chalmers, Otago Harbour, departure point of both Scott expeditions from New Zealand

stops.name: Cape Evans, Ross Island: the hut on the black sand
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18 January 1911 for the hut being made habitable (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'); the landing and construction ran from about 4 January, and the geography lens dates the stop 4 to 17 January, a range rather than a contradiction.
stops.campa: The shore party puts up a prefabricated hut fifty feet by twenty-five on a beach of black volcanic sand under Erebus, insulated with seaweed quilting, and moves in. A wall of packing cases divides officers from men, which Scott regards as natural and which visitors from other expeditions find remarkable. Twenty-five men will winter here, with a darkroom, a scientific bench and a stuffed penguin. The hut still stands: the stores on their shelves, the blubber stove black with soot, the seaweed quilting in the walls.
suggested_refs: The Cape Evans hut, conserved by the Antarctic Heritage Trust, one of the best-preserved sites of the Heroic Age

stops.name: One Ton Depot: thirty-one miles short
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 February 1911 and to 79 degrees 29 minutes south, more than thirty miles short of the intended 80 degrees (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'; depot-journey record cited in the dossier). That Oates urged pushing the ponies further and Scott refused is standard in the biographical literature and is reported by the dossier; it is not independently verified against a primary record in this pass.
stops.campa: The depot-laying journey is a bad education. The ponies flounder in soft snow and six of eight die. Oates argues for driving the animals on and killing them where they drop, and Scott refuses to buy thirty miles at that price. The depot goes down at 79 degrees 29 minutes, some thirty-one geographical miles short of the eightieth parallel where the plan had put it. A ton of stores, in the wrong place by a day and a half's marching. Fourteen months later three men will lie down eleven miles from it.
suggested_refs: The depot journey record of February 1911, on the siting of One Ton Depot

stops.name: Hut Point: the news from the Bay of Whales
stops.date_confidence: the encounter between Terra Nova and Fram in the Bay of Whales is attested to February 1911 (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'; dossier). Scott was not present: he was depot-laying, and this stop is placed where the news reached him rather than at the Bay of Whales, which is Amundsen's ground. The date of 22 February is an ordering device for the ship's return with the news and is not separately fixed in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: Terra Nova, coasting east, has found the Fram moored in the Bay of Whales and Amundsen's camp already building on the Barrier itself, sixty miles nearer the Pole than Cape Evans and stocked with ninety-seven dogs. The two ships' parties exchange visits and civilities on the ice. The news comes back to Scott by his own vessel while he is on the Barrier laying depots. He learns where his rival is, and that the man means to travel on skis behind dogs. Whether he changed anything in consequence is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Amundsen's base Framheim in the Bay of Whales, and the February 1911 meeting of Terra Nova and Fram

stops.name: Cape Evans: the winter journey sets out without him
stops.date_confidence: attested. The winter journey to Cape Crozier ran 27 June to 2 August 1911, tightening the loose '1911-06/08' of the chronology lens. The stop is placed at Cape Evans, where Scott was, and not at Cape Crozier, which is Wilson's, Bowers's and Cherry-Garrard's ground; Scott authorised the trip and did not join it.
stops.campa: On a night of the polar winter, Wilson, Bowers and Cherry-Garrard haul two sledges out of the hut and set off for Cape Crozier to fetch emperor penguin eggs, on the theory that the embryos will show the descent of birds from reptiles. Scott authorises the trip and stays. They are gone five weeks in temperatures below minus seventy, lose their tent to a hurricane on the cape, and come back barely able to speak. The eggs go to the Natural History Museum, which receives them without much interest.
suggested_refs: Apsley Cherry-Garrard, The Worst Journey in the World (1922), the account of the Cape Crozier winter journey

stops.name: Cape Evans: the motors go first
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24 October 1911 for the motor party's start from Cape Evans (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'). A coordinate in the geography lens placed this start near Hut Point, some 35 km south of Cape Evans, contradicting its own text; the Cape Evans pin is used here to match the attested claim.
stops.campa: The southern journey begins in pieces. Scott has built his transport on motors, ponies, dogs and men, in that order of use. The motor party takes the two surviving sledges out first, dragging loads toward the Barrier, and both machines break down within about fifty miles: cylinders cracked, a design never tested at these temperatures for this long. The men unharness themselves from the engines and go on hauling by hand. The machines are left standing on the Barrier where they stopped.
suggested_refs: The Wolseley motor sledges of the Terra Nova expedition, the first motor vehicles used in Antarctica

stops.name: Cape Evans: Scott marches
stops.date_confidence: dated to 1 November 1911 by the dossier's chronology, consistent with the framing of the Terra Nova timeline in Wikipedia. Amundsen's departure from Framheim on 20 October 1911 is well attested and is given here as context, not as a claim about Scott's knowledge, which he did not have.
stops.campa: Scott follows a week later with the ponies, the dog teams under Meares and Gerov behind him. Sixteen men are strung out on the Barrier in three groups moving at three speeds, an arrangement that requires the slowest to be met and resupplied on a timetable. Amundsen left his own base on the twentieth of October and is already south of where Scott starts, travelling on skis behind dogs with four companions and no ponies at all. Neither party has any idea where the other is.
suggested_refs: Scott's own journal for the southern journey, Scott's Last Expedition vol. I, chapters XIII to XVIII

stops.name: The Gateway, Beardmore Glacier: Shambles Camp
stops.date_confidence: attested to 9 December 1911 for the shooting of the ponies at the Gateway and to 11 December for the dog teams turning north (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'), both folded into this stop. The coordinate is corrected: an earlier fix at -83.9, 171 sat some 40 km up the glacier, whereas the Gateway, the snow-filled pass between Mount Hope and Cape Allen, is at 83 degrees 31 minutes south, 170 degrees 58 minutes east.
stops.campa: At the pass between Mount Hope and Cape Allen, where the Beardmore comes down onto the Barrier, the surviving ponies are shot as planned. The camp takes its name from the killing. A blizzard pins the party there for four days first and soaks everything they own. The meat is depoted for the return. Two days later the dog teams turn north for base as ordered, and from here to the Pole and back the men will drag their own sledges. Shackleton found this road three years ago and named the glacier for the man who guaranteed his overdraft.
suggested_refs: Shambles Camp at the Gateway, where the last ponies were killed on 9 December 1911
sources: ernest_shackleton.journey.json, stop 'Beardmore Glacier: the road onto the plateau'

stops.name: Polar plateau, 87 degrees 32 minutes south: five men, not four
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 January 1912 for the decision, at about 87 degrees 32 minutes south (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'); the last supporting party turned back on 4 January at roughly the same latitude. The geography lens had sited this turnaround at the lower Beardmore, roughly 400 km out, and conflated it with Tom Crean's solo walk of 18 February 1912 near Hut Point; both errors are corrected here and the longitude remains approximate.
stops.campa: On the plateau Scott sends back the last supporting party and takes not three companions but four: Wilson, Bowers, Oates and Petty Officer Edgar Evans. Bowers has already left his skis at a depot below and will walk the remaining seven hundred miles on foot beside four men on ski. The tent is built for four. The rations are made up in units of four, and every weighing, cooking and camping routine from here south has to be improvised. Teddy Evans, Crean and Lashly turn north the next morning with scurvy already coming on in one of them.
suggested_refs: Tom Crean's solo march of eighteen miles for help, Ross Ice Shelf, 18 February 1912, which saved Teddy Evans's life

stops.name: Polar plateau: the black flag
stops.date_confidence: attested to 16 January 1912 for the sighting (dossier chronology; the journal entry is printed in Scott's Last Expedition vol. I, ch. XVIII). The coordinate is approximate: the party was roughly thirty miles from the Pole that day and the exact position of the Norwegian marker is not surveyed.
stops.campa: Bowers sights something dark on the snow ahead, and it is a black flag lashed to a sledge bearer, with sledge tracks, ski tracks and the prints of many dogs running away from it in both directions. Out and back: the Norwegians have been here and have gone home again. Scott writes that day that the worst has happened, or nearly the worst, and that the Norwegians have forestalled them. There are still some thirty miles to walk south. They walk them, hauling the sledge over sastrugi.
stops.quote: The worst has happened, or nearly the worst. The Norwegians have forestalled us and are first at the Pole.
stops.quote_source: Scott's journal, 16 January 1912, in Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I, ed. Leonard Huxley (1913), ch. XVIII
suggested_refs: Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I, ch. XVIII, 'The Summit Journey to the Pole'
sources: Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I (1913), ch. XVIII, transcribed at Project Gutenberg 11579

stops.name: The South Pole: Polheim
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 January 1912 for reaching the Pole and to 18 January for walking to Amundsen's tent Polheim and reading the record inside (Wikipedia; Scott's Last Expedition vol. I ch. XVIII). One chronology entry had dated the Polheim record to 17 January; the journal places it under Thursday 18 January and that reading is followed here. Amundsen's party had arrived on 14 December 1911, thirty-four days before.
stops.campa: They reach the calculated position of the Pole, camp, and take their observations. The next morning they walk two miles to a small brown tent with a Norwegian flag on a broken sledge runner above it. Inside is a record of five men, Amundsen, Bjaaland, Hanssen, Hassel and Wisting, dated the sixteenth of December 1911, and a letter for King Haakon VII which Amundsen has asked Scott to deliver should the Norwegians not get home. They photograph themselves with a string on the shutter, five faces in a row. Then they turn round.
stops.quote: Great God! this is an awful place and terrible enough for us to have laboured to it without the reward of priority.
stops.quote_source: Scott's journal, 17 January 1912, in Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I, ed. Leonard Huxley (1913), ch. XVIII
suggested_refs: The Pole photograph of 18 January 1912, taken by Bowers with a string on the shutter
Amundsen's letter to King Haakon VII, left at Polheim for Scott to carry home
sources: Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I (1913), ch. XVIII

stops.name: Foot of the Beardmore: Edgar Evans dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 February 1912 (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'; Scott's journal). The coordinate carries the same correction as the Gateway stop: the mouth of the Beardmore is at 83 degrees 31 minutes south, not the -83.9 given earlier, which is well up the glacier. No autopsy was possible and the cause of death is contested between frostbite, exhaustion and head injury; none is asserted here.
stops.campa: Edgar Evans, the biggest and strongest man in the party, has been failing since a fall on the glacier: a cut hand that will not heal, frostbitten fingers, probably a blow to the head from a second fall, certainly a mind coming apart. On the seventeenth of February he drops behind, is found on his knees in the snow with his clothing loose and his hands bare, and dies that night in the tent at the foot of the glacier. No autopsy was possible and there has been no agreement since about what killed him. Four hundred miles remain to Cape Evans.
suggested_refs: The contested medical accounts of Edgar Evans's death, argued from Scott's and Wilson's journals alone
sources: robert_falcon_scott.dossier.md, on the absence of an autopsy

stops.name: Ross Ice Shelf: Oates walks out
stops.date_confidence: attested from Scott's journal to 16 or 17 March 1912, the entry itself hedging the date; the journal text as printed carries the words under c. 17 March. Oates's thirty-second birthday fell on 17 March. The coordinate is extrapolated from the party's position between One Ton Depot and the final camp; no site is recorded, since the body was never found.
stops.campa: Oates has feet gone black with frostbite and an old thigh wound from the South African war that has opened again in the cold. He asks Wilson whether he has a chance and is told that Wilson does not know. He asks the others to leave him behind and they refuse. On the morning of the sixteenth or seventeenth of March, his thirty-second birthday on him, he gets out of his bag, says he is going outside and may be some time, and walks into a blizzard in his socks. Everything known about that morning comes from Scott's journal.
stops.quote: I am just going outside and may be some time.
stops.quote_source: Scott's journal, c. 17 March 1912, in Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I, ed. Leonard Huxley (1913), ch. XX
suggested_refs: The Oates memorial cairn and cross erected by the search party in November 1912, near the presumed site
sources: Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I (1913), ch. XX

stops.name: The final camp: eleven miles
stops.date_confidence: the final camp was pitched about 19 or 20 March 1912, roughly eleven to twelve and a half miles short of One Ton Depot; sources differ on both day and distance and the difference is left standing. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from james_matthew_barrie.journey.json, where it is declared the atlas's conventional placement of the camp and not a surveyed point.
stops.campa: They pitch the tent on the twentieth of March with two days' food and one day's fuel, eleven miles from a depot holding a ton of stores, and the blizzard comes down and does not lift. The paraffin in the depots behind them had been leaking from its tins, so that even the fuel they reached was short of what the plan allowed. Two of the three can still walk. Wilson has the opium tablets Scott issued to the party at the head of the glacier. The tent is not struck again.
suggested_refs: The leather-washered fuel tins of the Barrier depots, whose evaporation losses were reproduced in later tests

stops.name: The final camp: the Message to the Public
stops.date_confidence: attested. The last journal entry is dated 29 March 1912 and the manuscript is held by the British Library as Add MS 51024-51042; the surviving manuscript is considered more authoritative for exact wording than Leonard Huxley's 1913 printed edition. The Message to the Public is undated within March 1912.
stops.campa: Scott writes on, in pencil, in a notebook held on his knees inside a bag whose foot he can no longer feel. He writes to Wilson's wife and to Bowers's mother, to J. M. Barrie, to his own wife, to the men who put up the money, and he writes a Message to the Public arguing that the causes of the disaster were not faulty organisation but misfortune in risks that had to be taken. He addresses that one to nobody in particular and to everyone, and asks in it that the dependants of the dead be looked after. The last entry in the journal is dated the twenty-ninth of March.
stops.quote: For God's sake look after our people.
stops.quote_source: Scott's final journal entry, 29 March 1912, in Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I, ed. Leonard Huxley (1913), ch. XX
suggested_refs: Scott's manuscript journals, British Library Add MS 51024-51042
Journals: Captain Scott's Last Expedition, ed. Max Jones (Oxford, 2006), collating manuscript against the 1913 text
sources: Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I (1913), ch. XX
British Library archive catalogue, cited in robert_falcon_scott.dossier.md
james_matthew_barrie.journey.json, stop 'The Ross Ice Shelf, the last letter from the tent'

stops.name: The final camp: the tent found
stops.date_confidence: attested to 12 November 1912 (Wikipedia, 'Terra Nova Expedition'). The thirty-five pounds of geological specimens and the arrangement of the bodies are from the search party's own account as relayed by the same source; the weight is given variously in the literature as thirty to thirty-five pounds.
stops.campa: A search party out from Cape Evans in November finds a few inches of tent pole standing above the snow. Inside are three men in their bags, Scott in the middle with an arm thrown across Wilson, and with them the journals, the letters, and some thirty-five pounds of geological specimens off the Beardmore that they had hauled to the end. Atkinson reads the burial service out of the wind. They take the papers and the rocks, collapse the tent over the bodies, and raise a cairn of snow with a cross made from a pair of skis.
suggested_refs: The fossil Glossopteris specimens recovered from the sledge, evidence for the former connection of the southern continents

stops.name: Observation Hill: the cross above Hut Point
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1913, with 22 January given by Wikipedia, 'Observation Hill (McMurdo Station)'. The cross was declared Antarctic Historic Site and Monument HSM-20 in 1972. That Cherry-Garrard proposed the Tennyson line is widely repeated and is not verified in this pass, so it is not stated.
stops.campa: The survivors carry a nine-foot jarrah cross up the volcanic scree of Observation Hill and set it in the summit rock, facing south over the Barrier toward the tent. Francis Davies, the ship's carpenter, made it out of expedition stores. On it are the five names and a line from Tennyson's Ulysses. It has stood there ever since, above what is now an American town of several hundred people with an airfield on the sea ice below it, and it is a protected monument of the Antarctic Treaty system.
stops.quote: To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the Observation Hill cross, January 1913, from Tennyson's 'Ulysses'
suggested_refs: Antarctic Historic Site and Monument HSM-20, the Observation Hill cross

stops.name: Oamaru: the news comes ashore at night
stops.date_confidence: attested to 10 February 1913 for Terra Nova's arrival at Oamaru and the release of the news (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'); the dossier gives February 1913 generally. The landing in the small hours and the refusal to identify themselves to the harbour authorities are standard in the accounts and are not separately verified here.
stops.campa: Terra Nova comes up the coast of Otago and puts two officers ashore in a boat at Oamaru in the small hours, ten months after the tent was found and eight after it was closed. They will not tell the harbour authorities who they are or what ship they came from. The news goes by cable to London under embargo until the families can be reached, and then it goes everywhere at once, in every language that has newspapers. The ship stands off the coast for two more days keeping her silence.
suggested_refs: The Oamaru harbour and the Central Otago cable route by which the news reached London

stops.name: St Paul's Cathedral: the King attends
stops.date_confidence: attested to 14 February 1913, with the King present (Wikipedia, 'Robert Falcon Scott'; dossier). The dossier cites BFI and Screenonline listings for contemporary film of the service; those pages were not independently re-fetched in this pass, so the filming is dossier-sourced rather than freshly verified. The Mansion House fund total of about seventy-five thousand pounds is from the dossier and is not re-verified.
stops.campa: A memorial service is held at St Paul's four days after the news lands. The King attends in person, which is not usual for a naval captain, and the crowd outside fills Ludgate Hill. Cinema cameras film the arrivals. Within weeks the Mansion House fund raises some seventy-five thousand pounds for the dependants and for a memorial, more than the whole expedition had cost to mount. Scott's last written appeal had asked for exactly that and had asked it in those terms. The two volumes of his journals, edited by Leonard Huxley, appear before the year is out.
stops.quote: But if we have been willing to give our lives to this enterprise, which is for the honour of our country, I appeal to our countrymen to see that those who depend on us are properly cared for.
stops.quote_source: Scott, 'Message to the Public', March 1912, in Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I, ed. Leonard Huxley (1913), ch. XX
suggested_refs: Scott's Last Expedition, 2 vols., ed. Leonard Huxley (London, 1913), the edition that shaped the public narrative
sources: robert_falcon_scott.dossier.md, citing BFI and Screenonline listings

stops.name: Waterloo Place, London: his widow's bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Statue of Robert Falcon Scott, London': bronze by Kathleen Scott, unveiled in 1915 by Arthur Balfour, funded by subscription among naval officers, Grade II listed 5 February 1970 (ref. 1357334), with a plaque naming Wilson, Bowers, Oates and Evans added in 1923. The exact day of unveiling is not given in the reachable sources and defaults to 1 January; sources place the statue within a few metres either side of this coordinate.
stops.campa: Kathleen Scott, a working sculptor and now a widow with a state pension and her husband's public estate to administer, makes the bronze that stands off Pall Mall: Scott in full polar clothing, ski poles in his hands, looking down the street. Naval officers subscribed the money. The inscription takes his own words about the hardihood, endurance and courage of his companions. Eight years later a plaque is added naming the other four men. She makes a second Scott the same year for Portsmouth dockyard, and a third, in Carrara marble, for Christchurch.
stops.quote: Had we lived, I should have had a tale to tell of the hardihood, endurance, and courage of my companions which would have stirred the heart of every Englishman.
stops.quote_source: Scott, 'Message to the Public', March 1912, in Scott's Last Expedition, vol. I, ed. Leonard Huxley (1913), ch. XX
suggested_refs: The Christchurch marble by Kathleen Scott, unveiled 9 February 1917, toppled in the 2011 earthquake and restored in 2017
sources: Wikipedia, 'Statue of Robert Falcon Scott, London'
Royal Museums Greenwich memorial record m4724

stops.name: Lensfield Road, Cambridge: a memorial that works
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Scott Polar Research Institute was founded in 1920 out of the Terra Nova fund's surplus, on the proposal of Frank Debenham, a geologist of the expedition; the Herbert Baker building on Lensfield Road dates to 1933-1934 (Wikipedia, 'Scott Polar Research Institute'). The founding month is not given and defaults to 1 January. The coordinate is corrected: the geography lens gave a point about 1.3 km west of the site.
stops.campa: Frank Debenham, a geologist of the expedition who had climbed Erebus in 1912 and come home wounded from the war, argues that the memorial to Scott ought to be a working institution rather than a stone. Every later reassessment of Scott's conduct, favourable and hostile alike, has had to be argued out of the archive that resulted. The Scott Polar Research Institute opens in 1920 on the expedition fund's surplus, holding the diaries, the photographs and the sledging gear, and moves in the thirties into a building by Herbert Baker on Lensfield Road.
suggested_refs: Roland Huntford, Scott and Amundsen (1979), the revisionist attack argued largely from this archive

stops.name: The geographic South Pole: the station with two names
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1956 for the construction of the station by Navy Seabees for the International Geophysical Year (Wikipedia, 'Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station'); the day is not given and defaults to the first. That the Ross Ice Shelf carries the final camp northward is attested; no projected year for the ice reaching the sea is asserted, since the widely repeated figure could not be confirmed from a source reached in this pass.
stops.campa: Forty-four years after the two parties reached it, Navy Seabees fly in and build a station on the geographic South Pole for the International Geophysical Year, and it is named for both men at once. The point Amundsen reached first and Scott reached second is now a permanently inhabited place with a runway and a winter crew. Polheim is somewhere under the ice, moving with it. Scott himself is still out on the Barrier, in the tent, drifting north a little every year inside a shelf that will one day calve and put him in the sea.
suggested_refs: Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, built November 1956 for the International Geophysical Year
